Swearers
SWAIR-urz
n. pl. (those who swear falsely; in Malachi 3:5, men who take the LORD's name to a lie)
From Old English swerian, to take an oath. In the Authorized Version false swearers renders a Hebrew participle from shaba, to swear, joined to sheqer, falsehood — men who swear a lie.

Biblical Definition

Malachi has been answering a generation that asked where the God of judgment is, and the answer comes as a list of the first men He will meet when He arrives: I will come near to you to judgment; and I will be a swift witness against the sorcerers, and against the adulterers, and against false swearers, and against those that oppress the hireling in his wages, the widow, and the fatherless. The false swearer stands in company — sorcery, adultery, wage-theft, the crushing of the widow. He is not a lesser offender who slipped into a serious list. To swear falsely is to call God as a witness to a lie, which is to attempt to make Him a party to it, and Scripture ranks it where that attempt deserves.

The third commandment governs the whole matter, and Zechariah sees the curse for it going out over the face of the whole earth on a flying roll, one side for the thief and the other for him that sweareth. Our Lord tightens the fence rather than loosening it. He does not abolish the lawful oath — He answered one Himself under adjuration, and Paul calls God for a record upon his soul — but He forbids the whole apparatus of graded swearing by heaven, by earth, by Jerusalem, by the head, by which men manufactured oaths they did not intend to keep. Let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay. A man whose plain word is good has no use for an oath ladder, and a man who needs one has already told us something.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): those who swear; in the bad sense, men who take an oath falsely or profanely.

expand to see more

SWEARER, n. One who swears; one who calls God to witness for the truth of his declaration.

SWEAR, v.i. To affirm or utter a solemn declaration, with an appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed.

PERJURY, n. The act or crime of wilfully making a false oath, when lawfully administered.

OATH, n. A solemn affirmation or declaration, made with an appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed.

PROFANE, a. Irreverent to sacred things; irreverent to God or to holy things.

Key Scripture

Malachi 3:5 — "And I will come near to you to judgment; and I will be a swift witness against the sorcerers, and against the adulterers, and against false swearers, and against those that oppress the hireling in his wages, the widow, and the fatherless, and that turn aside the stranger from his right, and fear not me, saith the LORD of hosts."

Zechariah 5:3 — "Then said he unto me, This is the curse that goeth forth over the face of the whole earth: for every one that stealeth shall be cut off as on this side according to it; and every one that sweareth shall be cut off as on that side according to it."

Matthew 5:34 — "But I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is God's throne:"

James 5:12 — "But above all things, my brethren, swear not, neither by heaven, neither by the earth, neither by any other oath: but let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay; lest ye fall into condemnation."

Modern Corruption

Profanity is treated as mere coarseness of speech, and the third commandment is reduced to a rule about vocabulary rather than about the truth of what a man says under God's name.

expand to see more

Two errors meet over this word. The first shrinks the third commandment to a list of forbidden syllables, so that a man who never says the word may swear a hundred false things and think himself clear. Malachi's false swearer is not a man with a coarse mouth; he is a man whose word cannot be trusted and who has dressed the untrustworthy word in God's name to get it believed. The second error runs the other way and reads our Lord's Swear not at all as abolishing the civil and ecclesiastical oath altogether — a reading the confession rejects, since Scripture records God swearing by Himself, Paul calling God to record, and the Lord answering when adjured by the high priest.

The 1689 Confession states the balance plainly: a lawful oath is a part of religious worship, wherein the person swearing in truth calls God to witness what he asserts, and it may be taken when imposed by lawful authority. What is forbidden is the vain oath, the false oath, and the whole trade in graded swearing our Lord names — by heaven, by the earth, by Jerusalem, by the head — which existed for one purpose, to sound binding while leaving an exit. The principle to recover is that a Christian's bare yes should carry the weight other men need an oath to borrow.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shaba (H7650), to swear, literally to seven oneself; sheqer (H8267), falsehood; Greek omnuo (G3660), to swear.

expand to see more

Hebrew shaba (H7650) — to swear; the root is seven, from the sevenfold witness by which oaths were bound.

Hebrew sheqer (H8267) — falsehood, a lie; joined to the participle it gives Malachi's false swearers.

Greek omnuo (G3660) — to swear, to take an oath; the verb our Lord restrains in Matthew 5 and James repeats.

Greek horkos (G3727) — an oath; that which is sworn, and in James the thing not to be multiplied.

Greek epiorkeo (G1964) — to forswear, to swear falsely; the sin Malachi's swift witness meets first.

Usage

"“a swift witness against... false swearers” — named beside sorcery and adultery."

"“every one that sweareth shall be cut off” — the flying roll, one side for each."

"“let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay” — the Christian's bare word as the oath."
